section: Part 1 — GitHub accounts: do you need a group account?
text:
Part 1 — GitHub accounts: do you need a group account?
Short answer: No. Everyone uses their own personal GitHub account.
Here is how it works:

One person creates the repository (the repo owner — probably you)
The owner invites other members as collaborators via Settings → Collaborators
Each collaborator uses their own GitHub account to push changes
GitHub tracks who made which change by their account

A shared “group” account is only useful if you want the repo URL to show an organization name (e.g. github.com/mylab/wiki instead of github.com/yourname/wiki). To do this, create a free GitHub Organization at github.com/organizations/new and transfer the repo there. This is optional — you can always do it later.
Summary:

Recommendation

Personal account, add collaborators

title: Group Wiki — Complete Setup & Contribution Guide
text:
Part 2 — What is a branch?
Think of the repo as a shared Google Doc. The main branch is the live published version of the wiki. A branch is your own private copy where you can make edits without affecting the live site.
main (live site)
 │
 ├── alice/update-methods    ← Alice editing methods.qmd
 └── bob/add-results         ← Bob adding a new page
When Alice is done, she opens a Pull Request — a request to merge her branch into main. Once merged, GitHub Actions rebuilds the site and the changes go live.
Why branches matter:

Two people editing main at the same time causes a merge conflict
Branches let everyone work in parallel safely
You can review changes before they go live

For a small group just starting out, you can skip branches and push directly to main. Add the branch workflow once 3 or more people are contributing regularly.

title: Continuum Model Tutorial — TBG and TMD Moiré Systems
text: This tutorial documents the continuum models used by the group for twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) and twisted transition metal dichalcogenides (TMD) moiré systems, including theory, code, and worked examples.

title: Continuum Model Tutorial — TBG and TMD Moiré Systems
section: Section 1 — Twisted Bilayer Graphene (TBG) Continuum Model
text:
Section 1 — Twisted Bilayer Graphene (TBG) Continuum Model

Introduction


Physics
The TBG continuum model (Bistritzer & MacDonald, 2011) treats each graphene layer as a Dirac cone shifted in momentum space by the twist. The Hamiltonian near valley \(K\) is:
\[
H_K = \begin{pmatrix}
h_+(\mathbf{k}) & T(\mathbf{r}) \\
T^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) & h_-(\mathbf{k})
\end{pmatrix}
\]
where \(h_\pm(\mathbf{k}) = \hbar v_F \boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\pm\theta/2} \cdot \mathbf{k}\) are the Dirac Hamiltonians of the top/bottom layers rotated by \(\pm\theta/2\), and:
\[
T(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{j=0}^{2} T_j \, e^{i \mathbf{q}_j \cdot \mathbf{r}}
\]
is the interlayer tunneling with moiré wavevectors \(\mathbf{q}_j\) connecting the Dirac cones. The tunneling matrices are:
\[
T_0 = w \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
T_1 = w \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \omega^{-1} \\ \omega & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
T_2 = w \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \omega \\ \omega^{-1} & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\]
where \(\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}\) and \(w \approx 110\) meV is the tunneling amplitude. The “chiral limit” sets the AA tunneling to zero (\(w_{AA} = 0\)) and retains only \(w_{AB}\).
The magic angle is where the lowest moiré band bandwidth vanishes and the density of states (DOS) diverges. For the chiral model:
\[
\alpha = \frac{w}{v_F |\mathbf{q}|}, \quad \theta_\text{magic} \approx 1.05°
\]

Key parameters:

Typical value
Description

1.05° (magic)

Note

Known issues:

The q-vector construction in the code assumes the chiral gauge; if you switch to a different gauge the tunneling matrices T[nu] must be updated consistently.
At exactly \(\theta = 0\) the code is singular (moiré period diverges); use a minimum of \(\theta \approx 0.3°\).

title: Continuum Model Tutorial — TBG and TMD Moiré Systems
text:
Section 2 — TMD Moiré Continuum Model

Introduction
Twisted TMD homobilayers (e.g., MoSe₂/MoSe₂, WSe₂/WSe₂) and heterobilayers (MoSe₂/WSe₂) host moiré flat bands in the valence band at twist angles of 1°–5°. These systems are distinct from TBG because the low-energy carriers live at the \(K/K'\) points of a massive Dirac (rather than massless Dirac) spectrum, and strong spin-orbit coupling locks spin to the valley. This section documents the group’s continuum model for TMD moirés.


Physics
The low-energy valence band near valley \(K\) of a monolayer TMD is described by a massive Dirac Hamiltonian:
\[
h_\tau(\mathbf{k}) = \begin{pmatrix}
\frac{\Delta}{2} & \hbar v_F (\tau k_x - i k_y) \\
\hbar v_F (\tau k_x + i k_y) & -\frac{\Delta}{2}
\end{pmatrix} + \tau \frac{\lambda}{2} \sigma_z
\]
where \(\tau = \pm 1\) is the valley index, \(\Delta\) is the band gap, \(\lambda\) is the SOC splitting, and the valence band maximum is at \(K\).
In a twisted TMD bilayer, the moiré potential from the registry variation modulates the on-site energy. Unlike TBG, the tunneling between the two layers is suppressed (due to the large momentum mismatch and the massive gap), and the dominant moiré effect is an intralayer moiré potential:
\[
H_\text{moiré}(\mathbf{r}) = V_0 \sum_{j=1}^{6} e^{i \mathbf{G}_j \cdot \mathbf{r}} + \text{h.c.}
\]
where \(\mathbf{G}_j\) are the moiré reciprocal lattice vectors and \(V_0\) is the moiré potential amplitude. The effective single-band model for the top-of-valence-band hole (spin-up, valley \(K\)) is:
\[
H = -\frac{\hbar^2 \nabla^2}{2 m^*} + V_0 \sum_{j=1}^{6} \cos(\mathbf{G}_j \cdot \mathbf{r} + \phi_j)
\]
where \(m^*\) is the effective mass and \(\phi_j\) encodes the local stacking geometry (MM, MX, XX high-symmetry points).
For a heterobilayer, the interlayer tunneling \(t_\perp\) is finite and must be included; it hybridizes the two layers and opens a gap at the moiré Brillouin zone boundary.


Usage

Set the twist angle \(\theta\) and material parameters (\(m^*\), \(V_0\), \(\phi\), \(t_\perp\)).
Build the plane-wave basis for the moiré superlattice.
Diagonalize to get the moiré valence bands.
Calculate DOS, effective mass, and Chern number of the flat bands.

title: DFT/ML Team Tutorial — 2D Materials, VASP, and ML Workflows
text: This tutorial documents the DFT setup, step-by-step workflows, example inputs for 2D materials, VASP bash scripts, and ML running procedures used by the DFT/ML team.

title: DFT/ML Team Tutorial — 2D Materials, VASP, and ML Workflows
text:
Section 1 — DFT Setup for 2D Materials

Introduction
Density Functional Theory (DFT) is the workhorse of first-principles electronic structure calculations. For 2D materials (graphene, TMDs, h-BN, etc.) there are specific choices of pseudopotentials, k-point sampling, vacuum spacing, and van der Waals corrections that differ from bulk calculations. This section documents the group’s standard setup so that new members can get a calculation running quickly and consistently.


Physics
2D materials are modeled using a slab geometry: the material sits in the \(xy\)-plane and a vacuum region of at least 15–20 Å is added along \(z\) to prevent spurious interactions between periodic images.
Key considerations:

Exchange-correlation functional: PBE (GGA) is the standard starting point. For band gaps and optical properties, HSE06 or \(GW\) corrections are needed.
van der Waals corrections: DFT-D3 (Grimme) or optB88-vdW are used for layered structures and heterostructures.
Spin-orbit coupling (SOC): Required for TMDs (MoS₂, WSe₂, etc.) to capture the valley-spin locking and large SOC-induced band splittings.
k-point mesh: For 2D hexagonal lattices a \(\Gamma\)-centered \(12\times12\times1\) mesh is a safe starting point. Convergence should always be checked.

The total energy per atom converges as:
\[
E_\text{tot}(N_k) \approx E_\infty + \frac{A}{N_k^2}
\]
where \(N_k\) is the k-point density. Always verify convergence of both \(E_\text{cut}\) and \(N_k\) before production runs.


Usage

Prepare the structure file (POSCAR) — see the example below.
Choose pseudopotentials from the group’s shared POTCAR library.
Set INCAR tags appropriate for a 2D calculation (see code section).
Set KPOINTS to a \(\Gamma\)-centered mesh with a single \(k_z\) point.
Run the ionic relaxation, then a static SCF calculation, then post-processing.

Typical calculation sequence:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=MoS2_relax
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=32
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=regular
#SBATCH --output=vasp_%j.out
#SBATCH --error=vasp_%j.err

module load vasp/6.3.2
module load intel-mpi/2021.5

# Run VASP
mpirun -np $SLURM_NTASKS vasp_std > vasp.log

# Check convergence
if grep -q "reached required accuracy" OUTCAR; then
    echo "Relaxation converged."
else
    echo "WARNING: relaxation did NOT converge. Check OUTCAR."
    exit 1
fi
Post-processing: extract total energy
grep "TOTEN" OUTCAR | tail -1 | awk '{print $5}'
Post-processing: extract band gap from DOSCAR
import numpy as np

def read_doscar(fname="DOSCAR"):
    with open(fname) as f:
        for _ in range(5):
            f.readline()
        header = f.readline().split()
        emax, emin, nedos, efermi = float(header[0]), float(header[1]), int(header[2]), float(header[3])
        energies, dos = [], []
        for _ in range(nedos):
            line = f.readline().split()
            energies.append(float(line[0]) - efermi)
            dos.append(float(line[1]))
    return np.array(energies), np.array(dos)

energies, dos = read_doscar()
threshold = 0.01
vbm = energies[dos > threshold][energies[dos > threshold] < 0].max()
cbm = energies[dos > threshold][energies[dos > threshold] > 0].min()
print(f"Band gap: {cbm - vbm:.3f} eV")


Bug Reports and Warnings






Warning



Dipole correction for asymmetric slabs. If your slab is not symmetric about the \(z\)-midplane (e.g. adsorption on one side), add LDIPOL=.TRUE. and IDIPOL=3 to the INCAR. Omitting this can shift the electrostatic potential and give wrong work functions and band alignments.








Warning



ISMEAR for semiconductors. Use ISMEAR=0 (Gaussian) with a small SIGMA=0.05 for 2D semiconductors. Using ISMEAR=1 (Methfessel-Paxton) intended for metals will give wrong occupations and a non-converging SCF.








Note



VASP license. The POTCAR files are licensed and must not be distributed publicly. Store the POTCAR library on the group cluster only, not in the public GitHub repo.


Known issues:

VASP 6.x changed the default for ALGO; set ALGO=Fast explicitly to avoid unexpected behavior on some systems.
Very thin vacuum (< 12 Å) causes image-interaction errors in charged calculations; always use ≥ 20 Å for charged 2D slabs.

section: Section 2 — ML Running Tutorial (Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials)
text:
Section 2 — ML Running Tutorial (Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials)

Introduction
Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) trained on DFT data allow large-scale molecular dynamics (MD) at near-DFT accuracy but at a fraction of the cost. This section covers how to train and run MLIPs — specifically using MACE (the group’s current preferred model) — starting from a DFT dataset generated by VASP.


Physics
MLIPs learn the Born-Oppenheimer potential energy surface \(E(\{R_i\})\) from DFT-labeled structures. The key idea is to represent the local chemical environment of each atom using equivariant descriptors that respect rotational, translational, and permutation symmetry.
The total energy is decomposed as a sum of atomic contributions:
\[
E_\text{tot} = \sum_i \epsilon_i(\{R_j : |R_j - R_i| < r_\text{cut}\})
\]
Forces and stresses follow analytically:
\[
F_i = -\nabla_{R_i} E_\text{tot}
\]
MACE uses an equivariant message-passing architecture (irreducible representations of \(O(3)\)). The loss function during training is:
\[
\mathcal{L} = w_E \|E_\text{pred} - E_\text{DFT}\|^2 + w_F \|F_\text{pred} - F_\text{DFT}\|^2 + w_S \|\sigma_\text{pred} - \sigma_\text{DFT}\|^2
\]
Typical weights: \(w_E = 1\), \(w_F = 10\), \(w_S = 1\).


Usage
Workflow overview:

Generate a training dataset of DFT-labeled structures (AIMD snapshots or active learning).
Convert VASP outputs to the extxyz format understood by MACE.
Train the MACE model.
Validate the model on a held-out test set.
Run MD with the trained potential using ASE or LAMMPS.

Prerequisites:
pip install mace-torch ase


Code
Step 1 — Convert VASP OUTCAR/vasprun.xml to extxyz:
from ase.io import read, write

# Read all ionic steps from a vasprun.xml (includes forces and energies)
traj = read("vasprun.xml", index=":")

# Write to extxyz format for MACE
write("dataset.xyz", traj)
print(f"Wrote {len(traj)} frames to dataset.xyz")
Step 2 — Train MACE model (bash script):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=mace_train
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --time=24:00:00
#SBATCH --output=mace_%j.out

module load cuda/12.1
source activate mace-env

mace_run_train \
    --name="MoS2_mace" \
    --train_file="train.xyz" \
    --valid_file="val.xyz" \
    --test_file="test.xyz" \
    --config_type_weights='{"Default":1.0}' \
    --E0s="average" \
    --model="MACE" \
    --r_max=5.0 \
    --num_radial_basis=8 \
    --num_cutoff_basis=5 \
    --interaction_cls_first="RealAgnosticResidualInteractionBlock" \
    --num_interactions=2 \
    --num_channels=128 \
    --max_ell=3 \
    --correlation=3 \
    --max_num_epochs=500 \
    --batch_size=10 \
    --valid_batch_size=10 \
    --lr=0.01 \
    --energy_weight=1.0 \
    --forces_weight=10.0 \
    --stress_weight=1.0 \
    --device=cuda \
    --seed=42
Step 3 — Run MD with trained MACE model:
from mace.calculators import MACECalculator
from ase.io import read
from ase.md.langevin import Langevin
from ase import units
from ase.io.trajectory import Trajectory

# Load structure and attach MACE calculator
atoms = read("POSCAR", format="vasp")
calc = MACECalculator(model_paths="MoS2_mace.model", device="cuda")
atoms.calc = calc

# Set up Langevin thermostat at 300 K
dyn = Langevin(atoms, timestep=1.0 * units.fs, temperature_K=300, friction=0.01)

# Attach trajectory logger
traj = Trajectory("md_300K.traj", "w", atoms)
dyn.attach(traj.write, interval=10)

# Run 10 ps
print("Starting MD...")
dyn.run(10000)
print("Done.")


Example
Active learning loop (bash outline):
# 1. Run short AIMD to generate seed structures
#    (see VASP INCAR with IBRION=0, NSW=500, TEBEG=300)

# 2. Train initial MACE model on seed set
mace_run_train --name="iter0" --train_file="seed.xyz" ...

# 3. Run MD with current model; flag uncertain structures
python select_uncertain.py --traj="md.traj" --threshold=0.1

# 4. Label uncertain structures with VASP single-point calculations
for d in selected/*/; do cd "$d" && sbatch run_vasp.sh && cd ..; done

# 5. Merge new labels into training set and retrain
cat seed.xyz new_labels.xyz > train_iter1.xyz
mace_run_train --name="iter1" --train_file="train_iter1.xyz" ...

# Repeat steps 3-5 until model errors are acceptable
Evaluating model accuracy:
from mace.calculators import MACECalculator
from ase.io import read
import numpy as np

calc = MACECalculator(model_paths="MoS2_mace.model", device="cpu")
test_frames = read("test.xyz", index=":")

e_errors, f_errors = [], []
for atoms in test_frames:
    e_dft = atoms.get_potential_energy()
    f_dft = atoms.get_forces()
    atoms.calc = calc
    e_ml = atoms.get_potential_energy()
    f_ml = atoms.get_forces()
    e_errors.append(abs(e_dft - e_ml) / len(atoms))
    f_errors.append(np.sqrt(np.mean((f_dft - f_ml)**2)))

print(f"MAE energy: {np.mean(e_errors)*1000:.2f} meV/atom")
print(f"RMSE forces: {np.mean(f_errors)*1000:.2f} meV/Å")


Bug Reports and Warnings






Warning



GPU memory. MACE training with max_ell=3 and num_channels=128 requires ~16 GB of GPU memory for large batches. If you hit OOM errors, reduce batch_size or num_channels.








Warning



Isolated atom energies (E0s). Always set --E0s="average" or provide explicit isolated atom energies. Using E0s=0 inflates the energy error by a constant shift and makes loss curves misleading.








Note



Train/val/test split. Randomly shuffle the dataset before splitting. If structures from the same AIMD trajectory end up in both train and test sets, your test errors will be artificially low.


Known issues:

MACE does not support mixed-precision training on all GPU architectures; use --dtype=float64 if you see NaN losses on older GPUs.
ASE’s Trajectory file is binary; use ase.io.read("md.traj", index=":") to convert to extxyz for analysis.

title: DFT/ML Team Tutorial — 2D Materials, VASP, and ML Workflows
text:
Section 1 — DFT Setup for 2D Materials

Introduction
Density Functional Theory (DFT) is the workhorse of first-principles electronic structure calculations. For 2D materials (graphene, TMDs, h-BN, etc.) there are specific choices of pseudopotentials, k-point sampling, vacuum spacing, and van der Waals corrections that differ from bulk calculations. This section documents the group’s standard setup so that new members can get a calculation running quickly and consistently.


Physics
2D materials are modeled using a slab geometry: the material sits in the \(xy\)-plane and a vacuum region of at least 15–20 Å is added along \(z\) to prevent spurious interactions between periodic images.
Key considerations:

Exchange-correlation functional: PBE (GGA) is the standard starting point. For band gaps and optical properties, HSE06 or \(GW\) corrections are needed.
van der Waals corrections: DFT-D3 (Grimme) or optB88-vdW are used for layered structures and heterostructures.
Spin-orbit coupling (SOC): Required for TMDs (MoS₂, WSe₂, etc.) to capture the valley-spin locking and large SOC-induced band splittings.
k-point mesh: For 2D hexagonal lattices a \(\Gamma\)-centered \(12\times12\times1\) mesh is a safe starting point. Convergence should always be checked.

The total energy per atom converges as:
\[
E_\text{tot}(N_k) \approx E_\infty + \frac{A}{N_k^2}
\]
where \(N_k\) is the k-point density. Always verify convergence of both \(E_\text{cut}\) and \(N_k\) before production runs.


Usage

Prepare the structure file (POSCAR) — see the example below.
Choose pseudopotentials from the group’s shared POTCAR library.
Set INCAR tags appropriate for a 2D calculation (see code section).
Set KPOINTS to a \(\Gamma\)-centered mesh with a single \(k_z\) point.
Run the ionic relaxation, then a static SCF calculation, then post-processing.

Typical calculation sequence:



Step
INCAR setting
Purpose




Relaxation
IBRION=2, NSW=100

Static SCF

Non-self-consistent band structure

LSORBIT=.TRUE.
Include spin-orbit coupling

# vdW correction

# Output

Example
Full VASP bash script — relaxation on SLURM cluster:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=MoS2_relax
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=32
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=regular
#SBATCH --output=vasp_%j.out
#SBATCH --error=vasp_%j.err

module load vasp/6.3.2
module load intel-mpi/2021.5

# Run VASP
mpirun -np $SLURM_NTASKS vasp_std > vasp.log

# Check convergence
if grep -q "reached required accuracy" OUTCAR; then
    echo "Relaxation converged."
else
    echo "WARNING: relaxation did NOT converge. Check OUTCAR."
    exit 1
fi
Post-processing: extract total energy
grep "TOTEN" OUTCAR | tail -1 | awk '{print $5}'
Post-processing: extract band gap from DOSCAR
import numpy as np

def read_doscar(fname="DOSCAR"):
    with open(fname) as f:
        for _ in range(5):
            f.readline()
        header = f.readline().split()
        emax, emin, nedos, efermi = float(header[0]), float(header[1]), int(header[2]), float(header[3])
        energies, dos = [], []
        for _ in range(nedos):
            line = f.readline().split()
            energies.append(float(line[0]) - efermi)
            dos.append(float(line[1]))
    return np.array(energies), np.array(dos)

energies, dos = read_doscar()
threshold = 0.01
vbm = energies[dos > threshold][energies[dos > threshold] < 0].max()
cbm = energies[dos > threshold][energies[dos > threshold] > 0].min()
print(f"Band gap: {cbm - vbm:.3f} eV")


Bug Reports and Warnings






Warning



Dipole correction for asymmetric slabs. If your slab is not symmetric about the \(z\)-midplane (e.g. adsorption on one side), add LDIPOL=.TRUE. and IDIPOL=3 to the INCAR. Omitting this can shift the electrostatic potential and give wrong work functions and band alignments.








Warning



ISMEAR for semiconductors. Use ISMEAR=0 (Gaussian) with a small SIGMA=0.05 for 2D semiconductors. Using ISMEAR=1 (Methfessel-Paxton) intended for metals will give wrong occupations and a non-converging SCF.








Note



VASP license. The POTCAR files are licensed and must not be distributed publicly. Store the POTCAR library on the group cluster only, not in the public GitHub repo.


Known issues:

VASP 6.x changed the default for ALGO; set ALGO=Fast explicitly to avoid unexpected behavior on some systems.
Very thin vacuum (< 12 Å) causes image-interaction errors in charged calculations; always use ≥ 20 Å for charged 2D slabs.

title: Continuum Model Tutorial — TBG and TMD Moiré Systems
section: Section 1 — Twisted Bilayer Graphene (TBG) Continuum Model
text:
Section 1 — Twisted Bilayer Graphene (TBG) Continuum Model

Introduction
At the “magic angle” (~1.1°), twisted bilayer graphene hosts nearly flat moiré bands that give rise to correlated insulating states, superconductivity, and orbital magnetism. The continuum (Bistritzer-MacDonald) model captures the low-energy electronic structure without requiring a full DFT calculation of the enormous moiré unit cell (up to ~10,000 atoms). This section documents the group’s implementation and how to use it.


Physics
The TBG continuum model (Bistritzer & MacDonald, 2011) treats each graphene layer as a Dirac cone shifted in momentum space by the twist. The Hamiltonian near valley \(K\) is:
\[
H_K = \begin{pmatrix}
h_+(\mathbf{k}) & T(\mathbf{r}) \\
T^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) & h_-(\mathbf{k})
\end{pmatrix}
\]
where \(h_\pm(\mathbf{k}) = \hbar v_F \boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\pm\theta/2} \cdot \mathbf{k}\) are the Dirac Hamiltonians of the top/bottom layers rotated by \(\pm\theta/2\), and:
\[
T(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{j=0}^{2} T_j \, e^{i \mathbf{q}_j \cdot \mathbf{r}}
\]
is the interlayer tunneling with moiré wavevectors \(\mathbf{q}_j\) connecting the Dirac cones. The tunneling matrices are:
\[
T_0 = w \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
T_1 = w \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \omega^{-1} \\ \omega & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
T_2 = w \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \omega \\ \omega^{-1} & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\]
where \(\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}\) and \(w \approx 110\) meV is the tunneling amplitude. The “chiral limit” sets the AA tunneling to zero (\(w_{AA} = 0\)) and retains only \(w_{AB}\).
The magic angle is where the lowest moiré band bandwidth vanishes and the density of states (DOS) diverges. For the chiral model:
\[
\alpha = \frac{w}{v_F |\mathbf{q}|}, \quad \theta_\text{magic} \approx 1.05°
\]


Usage

Set the twist angle \(\theta\) and the tunneling parameters \(w_{AA}\), \(\w_{AB}\).
Build the Hamiltonian in momentum space by expanding in the moiré reciprocal lattice.
Diagonalize at each \(\mathbf{k}\)-point in the moiré Brillouin zone (mBZ).
Plot band structure, DOS, Berry curvature, or Chern numbers.

Key parameters:



Parameter
Typical value
Description




\(\theta\)
1.05° (magic)
Twist angle


\(v_F\)
\(10^6\) m/s
Dirac velocity of graphene


\(w_{AA}\)
0–80 meV
AA site tunneling


\(w_{AB}\)
110 meV
AB site tunneling


\(N_\text{shell}\)
3–5
Number of moiré shells in basis


\(N_k\)
\(30\times30\)
k-point mesh in mBZ



Increase N_shell until the flat band bandwidth converges (typically shell 3 is sufficient for the flat bands, shell 5 for remote bands).


Code
TBG continuum model — Python implementation:
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import eigh

# ── Constants ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
hbar_vF = 2.1354  # eV·Å  (ℏ v_F for graphene)
a0      = 2.46    # Å     (graphene lattice constant)

def tbg_hamiltonian(k, theta_deg, w_AA=0.0797, w_AB=0.1100, n_shell=3):
    """
    Build the TBG continuum Hamiltonian at momentum k (in Å⁻¹).

    Parameters
    ----------
    k       : array_like, shape (2,)  — crystal momentum in mBZ
    theta   : float — twist angle in degrees
    w_AA    : float — AA tunneling in eV
    w_AB    : float — AB tunneling in eV
    n_shell : int   — number of moiré shells in basis

    Returns
    -------
    H : ndarray, shape (4*N, 4*N) — Hermitian Hamiltonian matrix
    """
    theta = np.deg2rad(theta_deg)

    # Moiré reciprocal lattice vectors
    a_moire = a0 / (2 * np.sin(theta / 2))
    b1 = (4 * np.pi / (np.sqrt(3) * a_moire)) * np.array([np.sqrt(3)/2, -1/2])
    b2 = (4 * np.pi / (np.sqrt(3) * a_moire)) * np.array([0, 1])

    # q vectors connecting the K points of the two layers
    q0 = (4 * np.pi / (3 * a0)) * np.array([0, -1]) * 2 * np.sin(theta / 2)
    q1 = (4 * np.pi / (3 * a0)) * np.array([np.sqrt(3)/2, 1/2]) * 2 * np.sin(theta / 2)
    q2 = (4 * np.pi / (3 * a0)) * np.array([-np.sqrt(3)/2, 1/2]) * 2 * np.sin(theta / 2)
    qs = [q0, q1, q2]

    # Tunneling matrices
    omega = np.exp(2j * np.pi / 3)
    T = [
        np.array([[w_AA, w_AB], [w_AB, w_AA]]),
        np.array([[w_AA, w_AB * np.conj(omega)], [w_AB * omega, w_AA]]),
        np.array([[w_AA, w_AB * omega], [w_AB * np.conj(omega), w_AA]]),
    ]

    # Build moiré lattice basis vectors {m*b1 + n*b2}
    G_list = []
    for m in range(-n_shell, n_shell + 1):
        for n in range(-n_shell, n_shell + 1):
            G_list.append(m * b1 + n * b2)
    N = len(G_list)

    # Hamiltonian matrix (4N × 4N: layer ⊗ sublattice ⊗ G)
    H = np.zeros((4 * N, 4 * N), dtype=complex)

    def idx(g_idx, layer, sub):
        return g_idx * 4 + layer * 2 + sub

    for i, G in enumerate(G_list):
        # Intralayer: Dirac Hamiltonian
        for layer in range(2):
            sign = 1 if layer == 0 else -1
            rot = sign * theta / 2
            c, s = np.cos(rot), np.sin(rot)
            kG = k + G + (q0 if layer == 0 else np.zeros(2))
            kx, ky = kG
            kx_rot = c * kx + s * ky
            ky_rot = -s * kx + c * ky
            H[idx(i, layer, 0), idx(i, layer, 1)] += hbar_vF * (kx_rot - 1j * ky_rot)
            H[idx(i, layer, 1), idx(i, layer, 0)] += hbar_vF * (kx_rot + 1j * ky_rot)

        # Interlayer tunneling
        for j, G2 in enumerate(G_list):
            for nu, q in enumerate(qs):
                dG = G2 - G - q
                if np.linalg.norm(dG) < 1e-6:
                    for a in range(2):
                        for b in range(2):
                            H[idx(i, 0, a), idx(j, 1, b)] += T[nu][a, b]
                            H[idx(j, 1, b), idx(i, 0, a)] += np.conj(T[nu][a, b])

    return H


def compute_bands(theta_deg, k_path, **kwargs):
    """Compute eigenvalues along a k-path."""
    bands = []
    for k in k_path:
        H = tbg_hamiltonian(k, theta_deg, **kwargs)
        eigvals = eigh(H, eigvals_only=True)
        bands.append(eigvals)
    return np.array(bands)
Plot band structure along Γ–K–M–Γ:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def make_kpath(points, n_per_seg=50):
    path = []
    dists = [0.0]
    for p1, p2 in zip(points[:-1], points[1:]):
        seg = np.linspace(p1, p2, n_per_seg, endpoint=False)
        path.extend(seg)
        dists.append(dists[-1] + np.linalg.norm(np.array(p2) - np.array(p1)))
    path.append(points[-1])
    return np.array(path), dists

theta = 1.05   # magic angle
a_m = a0 / (2 * np.sin(np.deg2rad(theta / 2)))
K_m = 4 * np.pi / (3 * np.sqrt(3) * a_m) * np.array([1, 0])
M_m = np.pi / (np.sqrt(3) * a_m) * np.array([1, 1/np.sqrt(3)])

kpts, tick_dists = make_kpath([[0,0], K_m, M_m, [0,0]])
bands = compute_bands(theta, kpts, w_AA=0.0, w_AB=0.110, n_shell=3)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 6))
for band in bands.T:
    ax.plot(band, color="steelblue", lw=0.8)
ax.set_ylim(-0.1, 0.1)
ax.set_ylabel("Energy (eV)")
ax.set_xticks(range(0, len(kpts), 50))
ax.set_xticklabels([r"$\Gamma$", "K", "M", r"$\Gamma$"])
ax.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.5, ls="--")
ax.set_title(f"TBG bands — θ = {theta}°")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("tbg_bands.pdf", dpi=200)


Example
Bandwidth as a function of twist angle (magic angle scan):
from scipy.linalg import eigh
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

angles = np.linspace(0.5, 2.5, 40)
bandwidths = []

for theta in angles:
    # Sample a few k-points in the mBZ
    k_samples = np.random.uniform(-0.05, 0.05, (20, 2))
    flat_eigs = []
    for k in k_samples:
        H = tbg_hamiltonian(k, theta, w_AA=0.0, w_AB=0.110, n_shell=3)
        eigs = eigh(H, eigvals_only=True)
        N4 = len(eigs) // 4
        flat_eigs.extend(eigs[N4 - 1 : N4 + 1])  # two flat bands near charge neutrality
    bandwidths.append(np.max(flat_eigs) - np.min(flat_eigs))

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(angles, np.array(bandwidths) * 1000)
ax.set_xlabel("Twist angle (degrees)")
ax.set_ylabel("Flat band bandwidth (meV)")
ax.axvline(1.05, color="red", ls="--", label="Magic angle")
ax.legend()
plt.savefig("bandwidth_vs_angle.pdf")


Bug Reports and Warnings






Warning



k-point folding into the mBZ. Momentum points must be folded into the moiré Brillouin zone before passing to the Hamiltonian. Passing points outside the mBZ does not cause an error but gives incorrect band ordering.








Warning



Basis size convergence. Using n_shell=1 (9 G-vectors) is insufficient even for the flat bands at the magic angle; use at least n_shell=3. For remote bands or Berry curvature calculations, use n_shell=5.








Note



Valley and spin degeneracy. The code above computes one valley (\(K\)). The \(K'\) valley is related by time-reversal: \(H_{K'}(\mathbf{k}) = H_K^*(-\mathbf{k})\). The total DOS and transport quantities should include both valleys and both spins (factor of 4).


Known issues:

The q-vector construction in the code assumes the chiral gauge; if you switch to a different gauge the tunneling matrices T[nu] must be updated consistently.
At exactly \(\theta = 0\) the code is singular (moiré period diverges); use a minimum of \(\theta \approx 0.3°\).



Additional Resources

Bistritzer & MacDonald, PNAS 108, 12233 (2011) — original TBG continuum model
Tarnopolsky, Kruchkov & Vishwanath, PRL 122, 106405 (2019) — chiral TBG model
TwistronicsLab code — open-source reference implementation
Song et al., PRL 123, 036401 (2019) — fragile topology of TBG flat bands

title: Continuum Model Tutorial — TBG and TMD Moiré Systems
text:
Section 2 — TMD Moiré Continuum Model

Introduction
Twisted TMD homobilayers (e.g., MoSe₂/MoSe₂, WSe₂/WSe₂) and heterobilayers (MoSe₂/WSe₂) host moiré flat bands in the valence band at twist angles of 1°–5°. These systems are distinct from TBG because the low-energy carriers live at the \(K/K'\) points of a massive Dirac (rather than massless Dirac) spectrum, and strong spin-orbit coupling locks spin to the valley. This section documents the group’s continuum model for TMD moirés.


Physics
The low-energy valence band near valley \(K\) of a monolayer TMD is described by a massive Dirac Hamiltonian:
\[
h_\tau(\mathbf{k}) = \begin{pmatrix}
\frac{\Delta}{2} & \hbar v_F (\tau k_x - i k_y) \\
\hbar v_F (\tau k_x + i k_y) & -\frac{\Delta}{2}
\end{pmatrix} + \tau \frac{\lambda}{2} \sigma_z
\]
where \(\tau = \pm 1\) is the valley index, \(\Delta\) is the band gap, \(\lambda\) is the SOC splitting, and the valence band maximum is at \(K\).
In a twisted TMD bilayer, the moiré potential from the registry variation modulates the on-site energy. Unlike TBG, the tunneling between the two layers is suppressed (due to the large momentum mismatch and the massive gap), and the dominant moiré effect is an intralayer moiré potential:
\[
H_\text{moiré}(\mathbf{r}) = V_0 \sum_{j=1}^{6} e^{i \mathbf{G}_j \cdot \mathbf{r}} + \text{h.c.}
\]
where \(\mathbf{G}_j\) are the moiré reciprocal lattice vectors and \(V_0\) is the moiré potential amplitude. The effective single-band model for the top-of-valence-band hole (spin-up, valley \(K\)) is:
\[
H = -\frac{\hbar^2 \nabla^2}{2 m^*} + V_0 \sum_{j=1}^{6} \cos(\mathbf{G}_j \cdot \mathbf{r} + \phi_j)
\]
where \(m^*\) is the effective mass and \(\phi_j\) encodes the local stacking geometry (MM, MX, XX high-symmetry points).
For a heterobilayer, the interlayer tunneling \(t_\perp\) is finite and must be included; it hybridizes the two layers and opens a gap at the moiré Brillouin zone boundary.


Usage

Set the twist angle \(\theta\) and material parameters (\(m^*\), \(V_0\), \(\phi\), \(t_\perp\)).
Build the plane-wave basis for the moiré superlattice.
Diagonalize to get the moiré valence bands.
Calculate DOS, effective mass, and Chern number of the flat bands.

Key parameters for MoSe₂/MoSe₂ (from literature):



Parameter
Value
Description




\(m^*\)
\(0.62 \, m_e\)
Hole effective mass


\(V_0\)
8–15 meV
Moiré potential amplitude


\(\phi\)
\(-89°\) (MoSe₂)
Moiré potential phase


\(a_0\)
3.32 Å
MoSe₂ lattice constant


\(\theta\)
1°–5°
Twist angle range of interest





Code
TMD moiré continuum model — single-band approximation:
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import eigh

# ── Material parameters (MoSe2/MoSe2) ─────────────────────────────────────────
hbar2_over_2m = 3.81      # eV·Å²  (ℏ²/2m_e)
m_star = 0.62             # in units of m_e
K_eff = hbar2_over_2m / m_star  # eV·Å²

a0_TMD = 3.32             # Å, monolayer lattice constant
V0 = 0.010                # eV, moiré potential amplitude
phi = np.deg2rad(-89)     # moiré potential phase (MoSe2)


def tmd_hamiltonian(k_vec, theta_deg, n_shell=4):
    """
    Single-band continuum model for TMD homobilayer moiré.

    Parameters
    ----------
    k_vec     : array_like shape (2,) — crystal momentum in mBZ (Å⁻¹)
    theta_deg : float — twist angle in degrees
    n_shell   : int   — number of moiré reciprocal lattice shells

    Returns
    -------
    H : ndarray, Hermitian Hamiltonian
    """
    theta = np.deg2rad(theta_deg)
    a_m = a0_TMD / (2 * np.sin(theta / 2))  # moiré lattice constant

    # Moiré reciprocal lattice vectors (hexagonal)
    b1 = (4 * np.pi / (np.sqrt(3) * a_m)) * np.array([1, 0])
    b2 = (4 * np.pi / (np.sqrt(3) * a_m)) * np.array([0.5, np.sqrt(3) / 2])

    # Build G-vector basis
    G_list = []
    for m in range(-n_shell, n_shell + 1):
        for n in range(-n_shell, n_shell + 1):
            G_list.append(m * b1 + n * b2)
    N = len(G_list)

    H = np.zeros((N, N), dtype=complex)

    # First-shell moiré reciprocal lattice vectors
    G1 = b1
    G2 = b2
    G3 = b2 - b1
    G_moire = [G1, G2, G3, -G1, -G2, -G3]

    for i, Gi in enumerate(G_list):
        # Kinetic energy (hole: negative sign)
        kG = np.array(k_vec) + Gi
        H[i, i] -= K_eff * np.dot(kG, kG)

        # Moiré potential: connects G to G ± G_moire
        for j, Gj in enumerate(G_list):
            dG = Gi - Gj
            for nu, Gm in enumerate(G_moire):
                if np.linalg.norm(dG - Gm) < 1e-6:
                    H[i, j] += V0 * np.exp(1j * phi * (1 if nu < 3 else -1))

    return H


def compute_tmd_bands(theta_deg, k_path, n_shell=4):
    bands = []
    for k in k_path:
        H = tmd_hamiltonian(k, theta_deg, n_shell=n_shell)
        eigvals = eigh(H, eigvals_only=True)
        bands.append(eigvals)
    return np.array(bands)
Chern number via Berry curvature (discretized BZ):
def berry_curvature_chern(theta_deg, n_k=30, band_idx=0):
    """
    Compute Chern number of a moiré band using the discretized
    plaquette method (Fukui-Hatsugai-Suzuki).
    """
    theta = np.deg2rad(theta_deg)
    a_m = a0_TMD / (2 * np.sin(theta / 2))
    b1 = (4 * np.pi / (np.sqrt(3) * a_m)) * np.array([1, 0])
    b2 = (4 * np.pi / (np.sqrt(3) * a_m)) * np.array([0.5, np.sqrt(3) / 2])

    kx_arr = np.linspace(0, 1, n_k, endpoint=False)
    ky_arr = np.linspace(0, 1, n_k, endpoint=False)

    def get_state(kx_frac, ky_frac):
        k = kx_frac * b1 + ky_frac * b2
        H = tmd_hamiltonian(k, theta_deg)
        _, vecs = eigh(H)
        return vecs[:, band_idx]

    F_total = 0.0
    for i, kx in enumerate(kx_arr):
        for j, ky in enumerate(ky_arr):
            u00 = get_state(kx, ky)
            u10 = get_state(kx_arr[(i+1) % n_k], ky)
            u11 = get_state(kx_arr[(i+1) % n_k], ky_arr[(j+1) % n_k])
            u01 = get_state(kx, ky_arr[(j+1) % n_k])
            link = (np.vdot(u00, u10) * np.vdot(u10, u11) *
                    np.vdot(u11, u01) * np.vdot(u01, u00))
            F_total += np.angle(link)

    return int(np.round(F_total / (2 * np.pi)))


Example
Band structure of MoSe₂/MoSe₂ at θ = 3°:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

theta = 3.0
a_m = a0_TMD / (2 * np.sin(np.deg2rad(theta / 2)))

# High-symmetry points of the moiré hexagonal BZ
b1 = (4 * np.pi / (np.sqrt(3) * a_m)) * np.array([1, 0])
b2 = (4 * np.pi / (np.sqrt(3) * a_m)) * np.array([0.5, np.sqrt(3) / 2])
Gamma = np.array([0.0, 0.0])
K_m   = (b1 + b2) / 3
M_m   = b1 / 2

kpts = np.concatenate([
    np.linspace(Gamma, K_m, 50, endpoint=False),
    np.linspace(K_m,   M_m, 50, endpoint=False),
    np.linspace(M_m, Gamma, 50, endpoint=True),
])

bands = compute_tmd_bands(theta, kpts, n_shell=4)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))
for band in bands.T[:6]:      # show 6 lowest hole bands
    ax.plot(band * 1000, color="steelblue", lw=0.9)
ax.set_ylabel("Energy (meV)")
ax.set_xticks([0, 50, 100, 149])
ax.set_xticklabels([r"$\gamma$", r"$\kappa$", r"$\mu$", r"$\gamma$"])
ax.set_title(f"MoSe₂/MoSe₂ moiré bands — θ = {theta}°")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("tmd_bands.pdf", dpi=200)
Chern number scan:
angles = [1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 4.0]
for theta in angles:
    C = berry_curvature_chern(theta, n_k=20, band_idx=0)
    print(f"θ = {theta}°  →  Chern number C = {C}")


Bug Reports and Warnings






Warning



Moiré potential phase \(\phi\). The sign convention for \(\phi\) varies between papers. The convention in this code follows Zang et al. (2022). If comparing to Wu et al. (2019), flip the sign of \(\phi\).








Warning



Heterobilayer vs homobilayer. For heterobilayers (e.g. MoSe₂/WSe₂), you must include both layers explicitly with different \(m^*\) and a finite interlayer tunneling \(t_\perp\). The single-band code above is valid only for homobilayers where the two layers are equivalent by symmetry.








Note



Chern number convergence. The Berry curvature calculation requires a fine k-mesh near singular points. Use n_k ≥ 40 for production Chern number calculations; n_k=20 is only for quick checks.








Note



Valley degeneracy. The model above is for valley \(K\) only. The \(K'\) valley contributes an equal and opposite Chern number. The total Hall conductivity from both valleys vanishes in the absence of time-reversal breaking; only one valley contributes under a circularly polarized optical field or in the presence of a magnetic field.


Known issues:

The plane-wave basis treats the moiré as perfectly periodic; strain and disorder are not included. For disorder calculations, a real-space approach is needed.
The effective mass approximation breaks down for large twist angles (\(\theta > 5°\)) where remote bands mix in; use the full two-band massive Dirac model instead.



Additional Resources

Wu, MacDonald & Martin, PRL 121, 257001 (2018) — first TMD moiré continuum model
Zang et al., PRB 106, 115416 (2022) — refined TMD moiré model with SOC
Shabani et al., Nature Physics 17, 720 (2021) — experimental MoSe₂/WSe₂ flat bands
Li et al., Nature 600, 641 (2021) — correlated states in TMD moiré
MoirePy — Python library for moiré continuum models (check for updates)
Fukui, Hatsugai & Suzuki, JPSJ 74, 1674 (2005) — discretized Chern number algorithm


Maintained by the Continuum Model team. Scripts go in scripts/continuum/ and figures in figures/. Add new parameter tables to the relevant section when new materials are calculated.

Part 2 — What is a branch?
Think of the repo as a shared Google Doc. The main branch is the live published version of the wiki. A branch is your own private copy where you can make edits without affecting the live site.
main (live site)
 │
 ├── alice/update-methods    ← Alice editing methods.qmd
 └── bob/add-results         ← Bob adding a new page
When Alice is done, she opens a Pull Request — a request to merge her branch into main. Once merged, GitHub Actions rebuilds the site and the changes go live.
Why branches matter:

Two people editing main at the same time causes a merge conflict
Branches let everyone work in parallel safely
You can review changes before they go live

For a small group just starting out, you can skip branches and push directly to main. Add the branch workflow once 3 or more people are contributing regularly.

## New experiment
